title: Wi-Fi Networks
summary: This technique covers gaining a first foothold by joining a wireless network, either an open network that a target device also uses or a secured corporate network reached with valid credentials. The defining constraint is physics: the actor must be close enough to the access point to associate and to keep a stable link, which makes this a close access technique rather than a remote one. Operators may position themselves physically near the site, or use a nearby dual-homed third-party system that has both wired and wireless connectivity as a bridge so no physical presence is needed. Once associated, the wireless segment gives the actor the same layer two view as any other client, which enables network sniffing and adversary-in-the-middle positioning for credential access and discovery. Wireless evidence is thin on the endpoint and rich on the network side. Controller and access point logs record association, authentication and roaming events with client MAC addresses, which is where a rogue or unexpected device appears, and RADIUS or network access control logs show which identity authenticated and with what policy result. Legitimate activity looks similar, so the differentiator is usually a client that authenticates outside business hours or from a location where no employee works, a new MAC address that is not in the asset inventory, or a dual-homed host suddenly bridging traffic.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker gets into your network by joining your Wi-Fi. They may use an open network that your staff also use. Or they may log in to your secured Wi-Fi with stolen credentials. To do this they must be close enough to reach the signal. Once connected, they are inside the network like any other device.
beginner.whyItMatters: Being on the Wi-Fi is often enough to reach internal systems, because many networks trust devices just because they connected. A connected attacker can watch network traffic, intercept logins, and find other devices to attack. A wireless network also reaches outside the building, so the attack surface extends into the car park and neighbouring offices. If you only watch servers and ignore wireless logs, these connections can go unnoticed for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the area and identifies the wireless networks they can reach from nearby.
They may connect to an open guest network that employees use with their work laptops.
For a secured network, they use stolen or guessed credentials, which are known as valid accounts.
If they cannot get near the building, they compromise a nearby third-party device with both wired and wireless connections.
That third-party device acts as a bridge, letting the attacker reach your Wi-Fi without being on site.
Once connected, they map the network, capture traffic, or sit between a device and the network to steal credentials.
beginner.example: Think of an airport queue where staff pass through a door that opens for anyone wearing the right badge. An attacker without a badge stands just outside the terminal, near enough to reach the same door with a pole. Or they bribe a cleaner who holds both an inside pass and an outside door key. That cleaner then props open a side entrance for them. Either way the attacker is now standing in the staff corridor, watching who types which door code.
takeaways: Joining the Wi-Fi can be the whole intrusion, so treat wireless as an entry point.
A nearby third-party device can bridge an attacker onto your network from far away.
Watch wireless controller logs for unknown devices and odd connection times.

objectives: Explain why connecting to a wireless network can count as initial access.
Describe the difference between open network access and access using valid accounts.
Explain how a nearby dual-homed device removes the need for physical proximity.
Identify the wireless and authentication logs that record association events.
Recognise follow-on behaviours such as network sniffing and man-in-the-middle positioning.
